title: The first good news (Genesis 3:15)
hook: even in the curse, a promise that the woman's seed will crush the serpent; Catholics see Christ and Mary here

segments.voice: Yesterday, where art thou: footsteps in the evening and a question that went looking for someone hiding. Did you stop one sentence before blaming? Day three hundred forty.

A statue of Mary stands in a side chapel. She's on a globe, hands open or folded, and under her bare feet, crushed flat, there's a snake. Sometimes it has an apple in its mouth. Statues like this turn up in Catholic churches and on holy cards, and they're easy to pass without a second look. But that snake under her heel is a Bible verse turned into stone. It comes from a dark moment in Genesis: the fruit eaten, the blame passed around, God about to speak the consequences. And right there, tucked into the sentence on the serpent, comes a promise.
screen: `MARY ON A GLOBE.` → `A SNAKE UNDER HER HEEL.` → `A VERSE TURNED INTO STONE.`

segments.voice: God turns first to the serpent, curses it to crawl on its belly, and then says this, in the Douay-Rheims: "I will put enmities between thee and the woman, and thy seed and her seed: she shall crush thy head, and thou shalt lie in wait for her heel." First, the order. Before God says a word to the man or the woman about pain and sweat and dust, God promises that evil won't win. The promise comes before their sentences. Second, the name. Early Christian writers such as Irenaeus read this verse as pointing to Christ, and the Catechism calls it the protoevangelium, the first gospel, the first announcement of the good news. The woman's seed is a descendant who will crush the serpent's head, while the serpent only strikes the heel. A wound, but not a fatal one. Third, the word she. The Hebrew says he, or it, the offspring. The Greek Old Testament says he. Saint Jerome's Latin Vulgate has ipsa, she, and the Douay-Rheims, translated from the Latin, follows it. Modern Catholic translations such as the New American Bible follow the Hebrew. Fourth, how the Church holds both. The Catechism reads the verse as pointing to Christ, the new Adam, and to Mary, the new Eve, who shares in his victory. So the Church doesn't need to choose between he and she: the Son crushes the serpent, and his mother stands with him. That's the statue. Not a woman fighting alone, but the promise of Genesis three, carved in stone and placed where you'd pass it.
screen: `A PROMISE BEFORE THEIR SENTENCES.` · `PROTOEVANGELIUM: FIRST GOOD NEWS.` · `HE IN HEBREW, SHE IN THE LATIN.` · `THE NEW ADAM AND THE NEW EVE.` · then, large: `SHE SHALL CRUSH THY HEAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find hope inside a hard moment. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something hard that's happening now, yours or someone else's. Don't pretend it's fine. Let it be as heavy as it is. Then look inside it, the way Genesis tucks a promise into the curse. Is there one small thing that's still good, still possible, still on its way? A friend who showed up. A door not fully closed. A morning that will come anyway. Hold that one thing next to the hard thing. If you pray, you can hand both to God. The bell holds the time.
Protoevangelium. Proto, first; evangelium, gospel. The name Christians give Genesis three fifteen: the first good news, spoken in the middle of the fall.
Your line: the promise came first. Today, when you have to deliver bad news, or hear it, look for the promise to say before it. Day three hundred forty.

notes: Douay-Rheims Genesis 3:15 quoted from memory; confirm.

Textual note: Hebrew hu (he/it), Septuagint autos (he), Vulgate ipsa (she; some Vulgate manuscripts read ipse). 'Most modern translations, Catholic ones included, follow the Hebrew' — the New American Bible and New Jerusalem Bible do; confirm.

Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.21.1) on Genesis 3:15 as pointing to Christ; dated 'since at least the second century'. Confirm. The term 'protoevangelium' itself is a later coinage; the script does not date it.
CCC 410–411: protoevangelium, Christ the new Adam, Mary the new Eve. Paraphrased; confirm.
howItsDone: Genesis 3:9–15, 20 is the first reading for the Immaculate Conception (December 8); confirm.
Statues of Mary on a globe crushing a serpent (Immaculate Conception, Miraculous Medal imagery): described generally; confirm.

Editor review (days 333-350): SERIOUS fix: the script said the promise came 'before the punishment', and the myth said God's first words after the fall went to the serpent; in Genesis 3 God first questions Adam and Eve (3:9-13) and curses the serpent (3:14) before 3:15. Now the promise sits inside the serpent's sentence, before the man and woman hear theirs (teach, screen head, myth, fork, trapdoor). Also replaced the banned 'Walk into almost any' hook and cut 'most modern translations', 'the first promise in the Bible', the undated 'since at least the second century' and a stock line.
